title: Roads in disrepair as state’s crime soars
full_text:
Victoria is leading the nation in car and home theft and burglary insurance claims, while almost half of state government-owned roads are in a “poor or very poor” condition and are deteriorating faster than the pace of repairs.
The data analysis conducted by the Insurance Council of Australia and the report on state government-owned and managed roads from the Auditor-General create fresh headaches for the Victorian Labor government ahead of the November election.
Both Labor and the opposition have put forward policies that aim to crack down on the high crime rates and fix the road network, with a particular focus on repairing potholes, in a bid to win voters in two areas of community concern.
A scathing report by the Victorian Auditor-General’s Office released on Wednesday concluded that the overall condition of state government-owned and managed roads was deteriorating, with about 48 per cent of the network in poor or very poor condition in 2024, compared to 39 per cent in 2021.
It revealed the Department of Transport and Planning had advised the government that funding levels had been insufficient to maintain or improve the condition of the roads.
“Victoria has a large and growing road maintenance backlog, where the network is deteriorating faster than the pace of repairs,” VAGO said.
State roads make up about 15 per cent of Victoria’s road network by length but carry most of the state’s traffic and freight, according to VAGO.
The department estimated it would cost $3bn a year to maintain road pavement condition at existing levels while replacing age-expired assets in its 2026-27 business case. Budget funding for road asset management in 2026-27 was $1.04bn, and Premier Ben Carroll recently announced an additional $352m towards repairing potholes.
Roads Minister Paul Hamer said he did not need a report to tell him the condition of the state’s roads needed improvement, and pointed to the $352m funding boost.
Meanwhile, analysis of Insurance Statistics Australia data conducted by the Insurance Council of Australia found Victoria was leading the country in both car and home theft and burglary insurance claims, with 12,300 claims regarding cars that had been stolen or broken into lodged in 2025-26, costing insurers $244m.
In that same year, 6200 claims for motor theft or burglary were made in Queensland, 5500 in NSW, 3500 in Western Australia, 1300 in South Australia, 400 in Tasmania and the ACT and 300 in the Northern Territory.
The majority of claims in Victoria were from metropolitan areas. More cars were stolen and broken into in Melbourne than in every other capital city in Australia combined, said the Insurance Council, which represents more than 50 general insurers.
The analysis also showed 3900 home theft or burglary claims were made in 2025-26 in Victoria, at a cost to insurers of more than $56m.
While it was a decrease on the 2024-25 figure of 5100, Victoria was still well ahead of all other states and territories.
Insurers in 2025-26 received 2300 home theft or burglary claims in Queensland, 1900 in WA, 1700 in NSW, 1400 in SA, 300 in Tasmania, 200 in the ACT and 100 in the Northern Territory. Insurance Council CEO Andrew Hall said a car was stolen or broken into in Victoria every 43 minutes, and a home broken into every two hours.
